::: {.callout-note}
**This chapter puts all fifteen previous chapters into one project.**

**Assumed knowledge:** everything. This chapter introduces exactly one new technique —
association rule mining — and otherwise assembles what you already have.

**The one idea to take away:** a finished project is not a model with a good score. It is
a **question, an honest answer, and a statement of what the answer cannot support.** The
last part is what separates a project from a demonstration.
:::

## 🎯 Learning outcomes {#sec-s16-outcomes}

By the end of this chapter you can:

1. Run a complete project from raw data to a deployable model.
2. Compute support, confidence and lift by hand, and mine rules with Apriori.
3. Read an association rule critically and reject a useless one.
4. Support a claim with a statistical test, not just a chart.
5. Compare several models honestly against a baseline.
6. Write up a project so somebody else can reproduce and challenge it.

# Part A — The whole pipeline {#sec-s16-a}

## 1. The project checklist {#sec-s16-topic-1}

**Before writing any code, answer four questions.** A project that skips this stage
usually produces a model nobody can use.

| Question | A bad answer | A good answer |
|---|---|---|
| **What decision changes?** | "we want to understand customers" | "we decide who gets the retention offer" |
| **What does success look like?** | "high accuracy" | "catch 60% of churners while contacting under 20% of customers" |
| **What data exists, and when?** | "we have lots of data" | "12 months of transactions, available the day after" |
| **What would make it useless?** | — | "if it needs data we only have *after* the customer leaves" |

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Fix the success criterion before you model"}
Choosing the target metric *after* seeing the results means choosing the metric your
model happens to do well on. **Write the number down first**, and keep it visible.
:::

### Demo 1 — the dataset, and the question

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(101)
n = 3_000

customers = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_id":   np.arange(1, n + 1),
    "tenure_months": rng.integers(1, 72, n),
    "monthly_spend": rng.gamma(4, 300, n).round(2),
    "support_calls": rng.poisson(1.3, n),
    "city":          rng.choice(["Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune", "Chennai"], n, p=[.35, .3, .2, .15]),
    "plan":          rng.choice(["basic", "standard", "premium"], n, p=[.45, .35, .20]),
})

# The truth we are asking the model to recover: churn rises with support calls,
# falls with tenure, and is higher on the basic plan.
risk = (-2.4
        + 0.42 * customers["support_calls"]
        - 0.030 * customers["tenure_months"]
        + 0.9 * (customers["plan"] == "basic"))
customers["churned"] = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-risk))).astype(int)

# Real data is never clean.
customers.loc[rng.choice(n, 120, replace=False), "monthly_spend"] = np.nan
customers.loc[rng.choice(n, 40, replace=False), "tenure_months"] = -1      # impossible
customers = pd.concat([customers, customers.sample(60, random_state=1)])    # duplicates

print(f"rows: {len(customers):,}   churn rate: {customers['churned'].mean():.1%}")
print(f"\nQUESTION      : which customers will churn in the next quarter?")
print(f"DECISION      : who receives a retention offer")
print(f"SUCCESS       : catch 60% of churners (recall ≥ 0.60) while contacting")
print(f"                fewer than 30% of all customers")
print(f"BASELINE      : contacting everyone catches 100% but contacts 100%")
customers.head()
```

## 2. Steps 1–3: clean, explore, prepare {#sec-s16-topic-2}

### Demo 2 — cleaning, with a report (Session 3)

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd

def clean(df):
    report, d = {}, df.copy()
    report["rows_in"] = len(d)

    d = d.drop_duplicates()
    report["duplicates_removed"] = report["rows_in"] - len(d)

    bad = d["tenure_months"] < 0                       # impossible before missing
    report["impossible_values"] = int(bad.sum())
    d.loc[bad, "tenure_months"] = np.nan

    report["blanks_before"] = int(d[["monthly_spend", "tenure_months"]].isna().sum().sum())
    d["spend_was_missing"] = d["monthly_spend"].isna()
    d["monthly_spend"] = d["monthly_spend"].fillna(d["monthly_spend"].median())
    d["tenure_months"] = d["tenure_months"].fillna(d["tenure_months"].median())

    q1, q3 = d["monthly_spend"].quantile([.25, .75])
    report["outliers_flagged"] = int((d["monthly_spend"] > q3 + 1.5*(q3-q1)).sum())

    report["rows_out"] = len(d)
    report["blanks_after"] = int(d.isna().sum().sum())
    return d, report

clean_df, report = clean(customers)
print("CLEANING REPORT")
for k, v in report.items():
    print(f"  {k.replace('_',' '):<22} {v}")
print("\nOutliers were flagged, not removed — high spenders are real customers.")
```

### Demo 3 — exploring, and forming a hypothesis (Sessions 7–8)

```{python}
#| label: fig-s16-eda
#| fig-cap: "Churn against each candidate driver. Support calls and tenure separate the groups; spend does not."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.2))
sns.boxplot(data=clean_df, x="churned", y="support_calls", ax=ax[0])
ax[0].set_title("Support calls")
sns.boxplot(data=clean_df, x="churned", y="tenure_months", ax=ax[1])
ax[1].set_title("Tenure (months)")
sns.boxplot(data=clean_df, x="churned", y="monthly_spend", ax=ax[2])
ax[2].set_title("Monthly spend")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Churn rate by plan:")
print((clean_df.groupby("plan")["churned"].agg(["mean", "size"])
       .rename(columns={"mean": "churn_rate", "size": "customers"})
       .assign(churn_rate=lambda d: (d["churn_rate"]*100).round(1)).to_string()))

print("\nCorrelation with churn:")
print(clean_df[["tenure_months","monthly_spend","support_calls","churned"]]
      .corr()["churned"].drop("churned").round(3).to_string())
```

**Three hypotheses, formed from the pictures:** support calls raise churn, tenure lowers
it, spend does little. Part C tests them properly rather than trusting the eye.

### Demo 4 — preparing, with a pipeline (Session 5)

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder

features = ["tenure_months", "monthly_spend", "support_calls", "city", "plan"]
X = clean_df[features]
y = clean_df["churned"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y)

prepare = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", StandardScaler(), ["tenure_months", "monthly_spend", "support_calls"]),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["city", "plan"]),
])

print(f"train {len(X_train):,} rows   test {len(X_test):,} rows")
print(f"churn rate — train {y_train.mean():.1%}, test {y_test.mean():.1%}  (kept equal by stratify)")
print(f"columns after preparation: {prepare.fit_transform(X_train).shape[1]}")
```

## 3. Steps 4–5: model and evaluate {#sec-s16-topic-3}

### Demo 5 — four models against a baseline (Sessions 9–11)

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score, roc_auc_score

cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
models = {
    "Baseline (majority)": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    "Logistic regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced"),
    "Decision tree":       DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, random_state=0, class_weight="balanced"),
    "Random forest":       RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=8,
                                                  random_state=0, class_weight="balanced"),
    "Gradient boosting":   GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
}

rows = []
for name, clf in models.items():
    pipe = Pipeline([("prep", prepare), ("clf", clf)])
    cv_auc = cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")
    pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
    pred = pipe.predict(X_test)
    proba = pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] if hasattr(clf, "predict_proba") else pred
    rows.append({
        "model": name,
        "cv_auc": f"{cv_auc.mean():.3f} ± {cv_auc.std():.3f}",
        "recall": round(recall_score(y_test, pred, zero_division=0), 3),
        "precision": round(precision_score(y_test, pred, zero_division=0), 3),
        "test_auc": round(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba), 3),
    })

print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
```

### Demo 6 — the threshold is where the business requirement is met

**Accuracy was never the goal. The goal was: catch 60% of churners while contacting under
30% of customers.** That is a statement about the decision threshold, not the model.

```{python}
#| label: fig-s16-threshold
#| fig-cap: "Recall and contact rate against the decision threshold. The shaded band is where both requirements hold."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score

best = Pipeline([("prep", prepare),
                 ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=8,
                                                random_state=0, class_weight="balanced"))])
best.fit(X_train, y_train)
proba = best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

thresholds = np.arange(0.05, 0.95, 0.025)
recalls  = [recall_score(y_test, proba >= t, zero_division=0) for t in thresholds]
contacts = [(proba >= t).mean() for t in thresholds]

plt.plot(thresholds, recalls, label="churners caught (recall)")
plt.plot(thresholds, contacts, label="customers contacted")
plt.axhline(0.60, color="green", ls="--", lw=1, label="required recall 0.60")
plt.axhline(0.30, color="red", ls="--", lw=1, label="contact budget 0.30")
plt.xlabel("decision threshold"); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()

ok = [(t, r, c) for t, r, c in zip(thresholds, recalls, contacts) if r >= 0.60 and c <= 0.30]
if ok:
    t, r, c = ok[0]
    print(f"Requirement MET at threshold {t:.3f}: recall {r:.1%}, contacting {c:.1%}")
else:
    closest = max(zip(thresholds, recalls, contacts), key=lambda z: z[1] if z[2] <= 0.30 else -1)
    print(f"Requirement NOT met by this model.")
    print(f"Within the 30% contact budget the best recall is "
          f"{closest[1]:.1%} at threshold {closest[0]:.3f}.")
    print("Report this honestly. Either the budget rises or the model improves.")
```

::: {.callout-important title="🔓 Report against the requirement, not against 1.0"}
"AUC 0.78" is a number. **"Catches 58.9% of churners within a 30% contact budget, against
a target of 60%"** is an answer. Only the second tells anyone whether to deploy.

**Notice that this worked example does not meet its own target**, and that this is left
in rather than tidied away. That is the realistic outcome: a model with a respectable AUC
can still fail the requirement the business actually set. The honest report says so and
offers the two real options — **raise the contact budget, or improve the model** — instead
of quietly switching to a metric that looks better.

A project that reports a missed target with the gap measured is worth more than one that
reports a good-looking AUC against no target at all.
:::

# Part B — Market basket analysis {#sec-s16-b}

## 4. Association rules {#sec-s16-topic-4}

**Association rule mining finds things that occur together.** *"People who buy bread and
butter also buy jam."*

Written as a rule: **{bread, butter} → {jam}**. The left side is the **antecedent**, the
right side the **consequent**.

**Three numbers judge every rule.** Compute them by hand once and they never confuse you
again.

| Measure | Question | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **Support** | how often does this combination happen at all? | transactions with all items ÷ all transactions |
| **Confidence** | when the left side happens, how often does the right? | support(both) ÷ support(left) |
| **Lift** | is the right side **more likely** than usual when the left happens? | confidence ÷ support(right) |

**Lift is the one that matters:**

| Lift | Means |
|---|---|
| **> 1** | they go together **more** than chance — a real association |
| **= 1** | independent — **the rule found nothing** |
| **< 1** | they go together **less** than chance |

### Demo 7 — by hand, on ten baskets

```{python}
baskets = [
    {"bread", "butter", "jam"},
    {"bread", "butter"},
    {"bread", "butter", "jam", "milk"},
    {"milk", "eggs"},
    {"bread", "jam"},
    {"bread", "butter", "milk"},
    {"butter", "jam"},
    {"bread", "butter", "jam"},
    {"milk", "eggs", "bread"},
    {"bread", "butter", "jam"},
]
n = len(baskets)

def support(items):
    items = set(items)
    return sum(items <= b for b in baskets) / n

left, right = {"bread", "butter"}, {"jam"}

s_left  = support(left)
s_right = support(right)
s_both  = support(left | right)

confidence = s_both / s_left
lift       = confidence / s_right

print(f"Rule: {sorted(left)} → {sorted(right)}\n")
print(f"  support(bread & butter)       = {sum(left <= b for b in baskets)}/{n} = {s_left:.2f}")
print(f"  support(jam)                  = {sum(right <= b for b in baskets)}/{n} = {s_right:.2f}")
print(f"  support(all three together)   = {sum((left|right) <= b for b in baskets)}/{n} = {s_both:.2f}")
print(f"\n  confidence = {s_both:.2f} / {s_left:.2f} = {confidence:.2f}")
print(f"     → when someone buys bread and butter, {confidence:.0%} of the time they buy jam")
print(f"\n  lift = {confidence:.2f} / {s_right:.2f} = {lift:.2f}")
print(f"     → they are {lift:.2f}× more likely to buy jam than a random shopper")
```

### Demo 8 — the trap: high confidence, no information

```{python}
# A rule about something almost everyone buys.
left2, right2 = {"milk"}, {"bread"}
c2 = support(left2 | right2) / support(left2)
l2 = c2 / support(right2)

print(f"Rule: milk → bread")
print(f"  confidence = {c2:.2f}   ← looks impressive")
print(f"  support(bread) = {support(right2):.2f}   ← but bread is in most baskets anyway")
print(f"  lift = {l2:.2f}")
print(f"\n  Lift near or below 1 means buying milk tells you NOTHING extra about bread.")
print(f"  A recommendation engine built on this rule would suggest bread to everybody.")
```

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Confidence alone will fool you"}
Any rule pointing at a very common item gets high confidence automatically. **Always
check lift**, and be suspicious of any rule whose consequent is your best-selling
product.
:::

## 5. Apriori on real-sized data {#sec-s16-topic-5}

**Checking every possible combination is impossible** — 100 products give more than 10³⁰
possible itemsets. **Apriori** avoids that with one observation: *if {bread, butter} is
rare, then {bread, butter, jam} must be rarer still*, so whole branches can be discarded
without checking.

### Demo 9 — mining rules with mlxtend

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import apriori, association_rules

rng = np.random.default_rng(102)
products = ["bread", "butter", "jam", "milk", "eggs", "coffee", "sugar", "tea", "rice", "oil"]

# Build 4,000 baskets with three deliberately planted rules, so we can check
# that the algorithm finds what we know is there.
transactions = []
for _ in range(4_000):
    basket = set(rng.choice(products, rng.integers(1, 4), replace=False))
    if "bread" in basket and rng.random() < 0.80: basket.add("butter")     # planted
    if "butter" in basket and rng.random() < 0.65: basket.add("jam")       # planted
    if "coffee" in basket and rng.random() < 0.75: basket.add("sugar")     # planted
    transactions.append(basket)

onehot = pd.DataFrame([{p: (p in t) for p in products} for t in transactions])

frequent = apriori(onehot, min_support=0.05, use_colnames=True)
# Deliberately NO lift floor here, so we can see how many worthless rules
# a permissive search produces.
rules = association_rules(frequent, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.10)
rules = rules.sort_values("lift", ascending=False)

print(f"{len(transactions):,} baskets → {len(frequent)} frequent itemsets → {len(rules)} rules\n")
out = rules[["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence", "lift"]].head(8).copy()
out["antecedents"] = out["antecedents"].apply(lambda s: ", ".join(sorted(s)))
out["consequents"] = out["consequents"].apply(lambda s: ", ".join(sorted(s)))
print(out.round(3).to_string(index=False))
```

### Demo 10 — did it find the rules we planted?

```{python}
planted = [({"bread"}, {"butter"}), ({"butter"}, {"jam"}), ({"coffee"}, {"sugar"})]

print("Checking the algorithm against the truth we built in:\n")
for ante, cons in planted:
    hit = rules[(rules["antecedents"] == frozenset(ante)) &
                (rules["consequents"] == frozenset(cons))]
    if len(hit):
        r = hit.iloc[0]
        print(f"  FOUND   {sorted(ante)} → {sorted(cons)}   "
              f"confidence {r['confidence']:.2f}  lift {r['lift']:.2f}")
    else:
        print(f"  MISSED  {sorted(ante)} → {sorted(cons)}")

useless = rules[rules["lift"] < 1.1]
print(f"\n{len(useless)} of {len(rules)} rules have lift below 1.1 — they tell you")
print("nothing, however good their confidence looks.")
if len(useless):
    worst = useless.sort_values("confidence", ascending=False).iloc[0]
    print(f"  worst offender: {sorted(worst['antecedents'])} → {sorted(worst['consequents'])}")
    print(f"  confidence {worst['confidence']:.2f}, but lift {worst['lift']:.2f} — below 1, so buying")
    print(f"  the antecedent makes the consequent LESS likely than for a random shopper")
print("\nFilter on lift FIRST, then read the survivors.")
```

# Part C — Making claims stand up {#sec-s16-c}

## 6. Test the claim, do not just draw it {#sec-s16-topic-6}

**A box plot showing two groups apart is a hypothesis, not a finding.** The gap might be
sampling noise. A statistical test puts a number on how likely that is.

| Question | Test |
|---|---|
| Do two groups differ in a **number**? | **t-test** |
| Are two **categories** related? | **chi-square** |
| Do three or more groups differ? | **ANOVA** |

**The p-value is the probability of seeing a gap this large if there were genuinely no
difference.** Small p-value → the gap is unlikely to be chance.

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ What a p-value does not mean"}
It is **not** the probability that your hypothesis is true. It is **not** a measure of
how big or important the effect is — with 100,000 rows, a trivial difference produces a
tiny p-value.

**Always report the effect size next to the p-value.** "Churners make 1.4 more support
calls on average (p < 0.001)" is a finding. "p < 0.001" alone is not.
:::

### Demo 11 — testing the three hypotheses from Demo 3

```{python}
from scipy import stats
import pandas as pd

churned  = clean_df[clean_df["churned"] == 1]
retained = clean_df[clean_df["churned"] == 0]

print("t-tests: do churners and retained customers differ?\n")
for col in ["support_calls", "tenure_months", "monthly_spend"]:
    t, p = stats.ttest_ind(churned[col], retained[col], equal_var=False)
    diff = churned[col].mean() - retained[col].mean()
    # Cohen's d — how big the difference is, in standard deviations
    pooled = ((churned[col].std()**2 + retained[col].std()**2) / 2) ** 0.5
    d = diff / pooled
    verdict = "REAL" if p < 0.05 else "not significant"
    size = "large" if abs(d) > .8 else "medium" if abs(d) > .5 else "small" if abs(d) > .2 else "negligible"
    print(f"  {col:<16} difference {diff:>+8.2f}   p = {p:<10.2e} {verdict:<16} effect: {size} (d={d:+.2f})")

# chi-square: is churn related to the plan a customer is on?
table = pd.crosstab(clean_df["plan"], clean_df["churned"])
chi2, p, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
print(f"\nchi-square, plan vs churn: χ² = {chi2:.1f}, p = {p:.2e}")
print(f"  → plan and churn are {'related' if p < 0.05 else 'independent'}")
print(table.to_string())
```

**Compare this with Demo 3's pictures.** The eye suggested three drivers; the tests
confirm which are real, and — importantly — how large each effect actually is.

### Demo 12 — what the model learned, checked against the tests

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

rf = Pipeline([("prep", prepare),
               ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=8,
                                              random_state=0, class_weight="balanced"))])
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

names = rf.named_steps["prep"].get_feature_names_out()
importance = pd.Series(rf.named_steps["clf"].feature_importances_, index=names)
print("What the model relies on most:")
print(importance.sort_values(ascending=False).head(6).round(3).to_string())
print("\nThe top features match the statistically significant ones. When they do NOT,")
print("something is wrong — usually a leaked column or a proxy for the target.")
```

# Part D — Delivering it {#sec-s16-d}

## 7. What you hand over {#sec-s16-topic-7}

| Deliverable | Must contain |
|---|---|
| **Repository** | code that runs from a clean clone, `requirements.txt` with versions pinned, a seed everywhere |
| **Report** | the question, what you did, what you found, **and what you could not conclude** |
| **Model bundle** | the full pipeline plus its metadata (Session 12) |
| **Application** | a deployed link a stranger can open |
| **Presentation** | eight minutes: problem, approach, result, limitations |

### Demo 13 — packaging the result (Session 12)

```{python}
import joblib, sklearn, tempfile, os, json
import numpy as np
from datetime import date
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score, roc_auc_score

folder = tempfile.mkdtemp()
path = os.path.join(folder, "churn_model.joblib")

proba = best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
thresholds = np.arange(0.05, 0.95, 0.025)
viable = [(t, recall_score(y_test, proba >= t), (proba >= t).mean())
          for t in thresholds if (proba >= t).mean() <= 0.30]
chosen_t, chosen_recall, chosen_contact = max(viable, key=lambda z: z[1])

bundle = {
    "pipeline": best,
    "features": features,
    "decision_threshold": round(float(chosen_t), 3),
    "trained_on": str(date.today()),
    "n_training_rows": int(len(X_train)),
    "sklearn_version": sklearn.__version__,
    "test_auc": round(float(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba)), 3),
    "recall_at_threshold": round(float(chosen_recall), 3),
    "contact_rate_at_threshold": round(float(chosen_contact), 3),
    "target_recall": 0.60,
    "contact_budget": 0.30,
    "known_limitations": [
        "trained on 12 months only; no seasonal effects captured",
        "support_calls is recorded after a complaint, so very recent calls may be missing",
        "no data on competitor pricing, which is likely a real driver",
    ],
}
joblib.dump(bundle, path)

loaded = joblib.load(path)
print(json.dumps({k: v for k, v in loaded.items() if k != "pipeline"}, indent=2))
print(f"\nmet the target? {loaded['recall_at_threshold'] >= loaded['target_recall']}")
```

**Note the `known_limitations` field.** It is the most valuable thing in the bundle, and
the field most projects omit.

## 8. Responsible delivery {#sec-s16-topic-8}

**Before a model touches a real person, answer three questions in writing.**

| Question | For this project |
|---|---|
| **Who could be harmed by a wrong prediction?** | a loyal customer wrongly flagged gets an unnecessary discount — cheap. A churner missed is a lost customer — the expensive error, which is why recall was the target. |
| **Does it treat groups differently?** | check the error rate per city and per plan, not just overall |
| **Would you be comfortable explaining a decision to the person it affected?** | if the answer needs "component 1 was low", reconsider (Session 6) |

### Demo 14 — a fairness check

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score

check = X_test.copy()
check["actual"] = y_test.values
check["predicted"] = (best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] >= chosen_t).astype(int)

print("Does the model perform equally across groups?\n")
for group in ["city", "plan"]:
    print(f"By {group}:")
    for value, sub in check.groupby(group):
        if sub["actual"].sum() == 0:
            continue
        print(f"  {value:<10} n={len(sub):>4}  "
              f"recall {recall_score(sub['actual'], sub['predicted'], zero_division=0):.2f}  "
              f"contacted {sub['predicted'].mean():.1%}")
    print()

recalls = [recall_score(s["actual"], s["predicted"], zero_division=0)
           for _, s in check.groupby("city") if s["actual"].sum() > 0]
print(f"Recall ranges from {min(recalls):.2f} to {max(recalls):.2f} across cities.")
print("A large gap means the model serves some groups better than others —")
print("worth investigating before anyone acts on it.")
```

### ❓ Check yourself

**Q1.** A rule has confidence 0.85 and lift 1.02. Is it useful?

- (a) Yes, 85% confidence is high.
- (b) **No — lift near 1 means the consequent is no more likely than usual.**
- (c) Only if support is high.

**Q2.** Why fix the success criterion before modelling?

- (a) It is required by scikit-learn.
- (b) **Otherwise you choose the metric your model happens to do well on.**
- (c) It speeds up training.

**Q3.** Your t-test gives p = 0.0001 and Cohen's d = 0.04. What do you report?

- (a) A highly significant, important finding.
- (b) **A real but negligibly small difference — significant because the sample is large,
  not because it matters.**
- (c) Nothing; the p-value is too small.

**Q4.** The model's most important feature is one the statistical tests found
insignificant. What should you suspect?

- (a) The tests were wrong.
- (b) **Leakage, or a proxy for the target — investigate that column.**
- (c) Nothing; models see things tests cannot.

**Q5.** What is the most valuable section of a project report?

- (a) The accuracy figure.
- (b) The code listing.
- (c) **What the result cannot support, and why.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"}
**A1 — (b).** Demo 8 measured exactly this case.

**A2 — (b).** The criterion is a commitment; chosen afterwards it is a rationalisation.

**A3 — (b).** With enough rows any difference becomes significant. The effect size is
what says whether anyone should care.

**A4 — (b).** Demo 12's closing note. This mismatch is one of the most reliable leakage
detectors there is.

**A5 — (c).** It is what lets somebody else use the result safely — and it is the section
that is almost always missing.
:::

# 🎯 Capstone project {#sec-s16-tasks}

::: {.callout-note title="✏️ Your project"}
**Task 1 — Frame it.** Choose a dataset. Write the four answers from Demo 1: the
decision, the success criterion **with a number**, the data available, and what would
make the model useless. **Fix these before writing code.**

**Task 2 — Clean and explore.** Produce a cleaning report and an EDA section that ends
with three written hypotheses.

**Task 3 — Test the hypotheses.** For each, run the appropriate test and report the
p-value **and** the effect size. Say which survived.

**Task 4 — Model.** Compare at least four models against a baseline, cross-validated with
the spread reported. Tune the best one without touching the test set.

**Task 5 — Meet the requirement.** Choose the decision threshold that satisfies your
Task 1 criterion, **or report honestly that no threshold does.**

**Task 6 — Mine the rules.** If your data has transactions, run Apriori and report the
three most useful rules by lift. Explain why each is actionable.

**Task 7 — Deliver.** Bundle the pipeline with metadata and limitations, deploy a
Streamlit app, and write the report.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="✅ A capstone that passes"}
- [ ] Runs from a clean clone, first try, with versions pinned
- [ ] States a success criterion that was fixed **before** the modelling
- [ ] Beats a named baseline, with the baseline's score printed
- [ ] Reports at least one thing that was tried and did not work
- [ ] Supports every claim with a test **and** an effect size, not just a chart
- [ ] Has a deployed link a stranger can open
- [ ] Names who could be harmed by a wrong prediction, and checks group fairness
- [ ] **Says clearly what the result cannot support**
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="✅ Before you finish the course"}
Sixteen chapters, one sentence each:

1. Data science turns recorded facts into decisions
2. Get data in with pandas; look before you touch
3. Clean in order — duplicates, impossible, missing, noise, outliers, text
4. Join carefully, and check the row count every time
5. Split before you scale; encode text; never leak
6. Fewer columns is often better; say what the reduction cost
7. Report a centre **and** a spread **and** a shape
8. Every chart answers a question you asked first
9. A model is a rule learned from examples; beat a baseline
10. Clustering has no answer key — justify the result instead
11. One split is one opinion; cross-validate and report the spread
12. Save the pipeline, validate inputs, watch for drift
13. Big data is a symptom, not a size; try chunking first
14. Map, shuffle, reduce — and the shuffle is the expensive part
15. NoSQL trades schema for flexibility; aggregate in the database
16. A finished project states what it cannot support
:::
